clinicalPearls: Hookworm infection is caused mainly by Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, soil-transmitted nematodes and a leading cause of iron-deficiency anaemia in the tropics
Infective larvae in warm, moist soil penetrate intact skin, classically the feet, producing a localised itchy papulovesicular rash known as ground itch
Migrating larvae passing through the lungs can cause a transient cough and wheeze with pulmonary eosinophilia (Loeffler syndrome)
Adult worms attach to the small-intestinal mucosa and feed on blood, and the chronic intestinal blood loss produces microcytic hypochromic anaemia and hypoproteinaemia proportional to worm burden
Heavy infection in children can impair growth, development and cognition, while in pregnancy it worsens maternal anaemia
Diagnosis is by finding the characteristic thin-shelled eggs on stool microscopy, with concentration or quantitative techniques used to estimate burden
Albendazole or mebendazole is the mainstay of treatment, alongside iron replacement to correct anaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Hookworm eggs passed in faeces hatch in warm, moist soil into infective filariform larvae that penetrate the skin, enter the circulation and are carried to the lungs. There they break into the alveoli, ascend the airways, are swallowed, and mature into adults that attach to the small-intestinal mucosa. Using cutting plates or teeth, the adults erode mucosal capillaries and ingest blood, while anticoagulant secretions promote continued oozing from the attachment site. The resulting chronic gastrointestinal blood and protein loss depletes iron stores, causing microcytic hypochromic anaemia and hypoalbuminaemia with oedema when the burden is heavy and dietary iron intake is poor; larval migration through skin and lung accounts for the earlier cutaneous and pulmonary manifestations.
additionalDifferentials: Other soil-transmitted helminthiases such as ascariasis and trichuriasis
Iron-deficiency anaemia from other causes of chronic blood loss
Coeliac disease and other malabsorptive states
Peptic ulcer disease or other gastrointestinal bleeding
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for characteristic hookworm eggs
Faecal egg quantification such as Kato-Katz to estimate worm burden
Full blood count and film showing microcytic hypochromic anaemia
Serum albumin to assess protein loss
Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia during larval migration
redFlags: Severe symptomatic anaemia with cardiac decompensation
Heavy infection in a young child with growth or developmental impairment
Anaemia in pregnancy with risk to mother and fetus
reference.prognosis: Excellent with anthelmintic treatment and iron replacement; anaemia and protein loss are reversible, though reinfection is common in endemic areas without improved sanitation and footwear.
pitfalls: Correcting iron-deficiency anaemia without seeking and treating the underlying hookworm burden
Overlooking the diagnosis in returning travellers with unexplained eosinophilia
Assuming a single deworming dose confers lasting protection where reinfection is ongoing
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Give anthelmintic therapy with a benzimidazole such as albendazole or mebendazole to eradicate the adult worms
Correct iron-deficiency anaemia with oral or parenteral iron replacement and ensure adequate protein and nutrition
Confirm cure of heavy or symptomatic infection with follow-up stool examination
In pregnancy, treat maternal anaemia and give anthelmintics per local guidance after the first trimester
Prevent reinfection through footwear, sanitation and hygiene, with community mass deworming in endemic areas
Manage severe symptomatic anaemia with blood transfusion where haemodynamically indicated, alongside iron replacement
